title: Doe Run commits to ‘cleaner smelting’ tech boost in focus on sustainability – Batteries International
content: Breakthrough ‘cleaner smelting’ technology developed by US lead miner and recycler the Doe Run Company is to be further improved over the next year as the firm enhances its sustainability credentials. The firm’s ACL HydroMet Process (ACL), in development for 15 years, has the potential to help fuel additional critical minerals production in the US state of Missouri, Doe Run president and CEO Matthew Wohl said on October 5. A pilot plant has already proven that the proprietary technology can extract a versatile array of critical minerals, including cobalt, copper, germanium, nickel, zinc, lead, antimony and tin, Wohl said. In a letter published alongside the firm’s 17th annual sustainability report, he said once ACL enters full commercial production, it will allow Doe Run to generate a greater volume of valuable resources from the same amount of mined and recycled material. Liquid-based chemistry Existing milling and mineral processing techniques require Doe Run to be highly selective about headings being mined and to sort material underground before it reaches the mills — costing money and higher costs increase the ore grade needed to cover expenses. However, ACL “changes that equation”, Wohl said. Unlike traditional smelting, which requires immense heat, energy and emits significant greenhouse gases, ACL uses liquid-based chemistry, specifically an ammonium chloride solution, to extract a wider range of metals from mineral concentrates, recycled batteries, pyrometallurgical slag and mining chat and tailings. Doe Run claims the technology achieves what no other hydrometallurgical process that the company knows of currently in use can do: recover multiple critical minerals (including copper, zinc, cobalt, nickel, lead, tin, antimony, and germanium) with one process in a single facility, with significantly lower air emissions and a smaller carbon footprint. The chloride-based solutions are recycled within the process, minimising liquid waste and reducing operating costs compared to conventional methods. Wohl said as the process can be fed by a lower grade bulk concentrate, the sorting and separation performed underground today will no longer be necessary, meaning less time and less cost to bring material to the surface. ‘Lower costs’ “Lower operating costs also support economically mining lower-grade ore, while enabling recovery of minerals that are difficult to recover with current approaches, including cobalt, nickel, and germanium. “By lowering costs and recovering more value from the same ore bodies, we can extend the life of our mines and sustain the jobs of the people who work them.” Meanwhile, Doe Run continues to modernise recycling operations to meet changing market needs. Over 30 years ago, Doe Run transformed a primary lead smelter into a plant that recycles lead batteries and other lead-bearing materials — the Buick Resource Recycling Facility — one of the nation’s largest lead recycling operations. Wohl said the company’s engineers are now pushing ahead with a modernisation plan that incorporates ACL into its current recycling operations in addition to using off-the-shelf technology. Critical minerals The result is improved operating conditions for employees, fewer emissions, lower operating costs, and better recovery of minerals, particularly tin and antimony, that arrive at the company’s receiving dock. “Through our pilot plant, we have proven that our proprietary technology can extract a versatile array of critical minerals, including cobalt, copper, germanium, nickel, zinc, lead, antimony, and tin,” Wohl said. “These minerals are strategically important to national security, commercial production of goods, and economic well-being, and the US continues to depend heavily on foreign supply for many of them. The process can also pull valuable resources from what is currently considered waste, strengthening US supply and supporting environmental cleanup.” Doe Run is proud of keeping 100% of its copper product in North America for processing, reducing foreign dependency and cutting emissions associated with long-distance freight. The company is also continuing domestic production of zinc, keeping the vast majority of its zinc in North America for production — and said its recycling operations are essential to strengthening US resilience by helping support domestic battery supply chains. But Wohl said lead remains a Doe Run staple — its strategic and economic value confirmed by being designated by the US as a critical mineral last year — and the company is the country’s top lead concentrate producer. “Our product is among the cleanest in the world and is trusted across the industry. We continue to sell 100% of our production.” Doe Run’s sustainability report is online . title: As electric semi truck race heats up, SoCal is getting another charging hub
content:
As record-breaking diesel prices drive demand for electric big rigs, so, too is the demand for commercial truck charging climbing. To meet that demand, EV Realty as announced a new, Inland Empire site for its next electric semi truck charging hub.
With companies like BYD and Volvo about to roll out their third generation electric trucks and the Tesla Semi allegedly in production after nearly a decade of waiting, it seems like American fleets are starting to understand what the rest of the world has already figured out: predictable fuel costs means predictable operating budgets, and predictable budgets means less volatile consumer pricing and a happier, less guillotine-y populace. To that end, fleets are buying EVs in record numbers – much to the dismay of that News Corp/Fox-owned rag, the Wall Street Journal, who are so desperate to spread that narrative that they’ve published essentially the same article under different bylines several times. (lol)
Keeping those fleets topped off with electric fuel is going to be the challenge now, and a number of companies are stepping up with commercial charging hubs designed with broad turning areas, easy highway access, and trailer-friendly pull-through designs built specifically to meet the needs of big rig drivers.
The latest new site, acquired this week by EV Realty, is set to located at 2151 E. Philadelphia Street in what the company calls, “the West Coast’s largest and most concentrated warehousing submarket,” making it an ideal site to service local freight and logistics operations.
The property has excellent access to the east-west SR-60 and north-south I-15 freeways and is well-positioned to provide charging for fleets serving the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach as well as the intermodal facilities in Los Angeles and San Bernardino, and is located just three miles from Ontario International Airport – one of the top 10 cargo airports in the country and home to major air freight operations for companies like UPS and FedEx.
Location, location, location
“Ontario sits at the convergence of the nation’s largest container gateway and the densest warehouse cluster in North America. This part of Southern California is among the most important freight hubs in the world and is the epicenter of truck electrification for this country,” said EV Realty CEO Patrick Sullivan. “When this site comes online, EV Realty will have 27 MW of simultaneous truck charging capacity between the ports and the Inland Empire. This is how we start to see real scale – finding power in the right locations and building infrastructure to meet growing demand.”
Grid capacity in general in Southern California is severely constrained in many areas, a fact that EV Realty believes underscores the value of this high-capacity site for fleet operators that need power in the region
Top comment by BlueStrawberry
Grid capacity limits have been a fear tactic as long as I can remember. I grew up in Connecticut, and I remember in the late 70s and early 80s there was talk about how we desperately needed to upgrade the grid or the southeast portion of the state could see brown outs by 2000. This of course, is because power companies only build for what's needed now, and then they use the constricted capacity to generate fear, which gets them higher pricing and less oversight when they do expand.
So now we have another need to expand the grid, and the fossil fuel industry is happy to point out that the current grid can't handle what will be needed. Of course it can't. That's by design! But it will handle it when it's built. Plus, if we distribute more solar throughout the grid it will need less expansion. There's no need to deliver power over long distances if it's produced locally!
The company expects construction at the site to being early next year, with chargers coming online before 2028.

title: Why plugging ships into the grid can cost more than running onboard generators
content: A ship can switch off its generators, burn less fuel and reduce pollution while docked, yet still face a higher power bill. That is the financial challenge surrounding Portsmouth International Port’s new shore power system. The port has launched the UK’s first high-voltage, multi-berth installation, allowing docked ships to connect to grid electricity instead of generating power onboard. It supports Portsmouth’s ambition to become a net-zero facility, improve local air quality and contribute to the wider decarbonization of shipping. However, high UK electricity prices complicate the economics. Shore power can replace fuel-burning generators without delivering the savings operators might expect, while rising grid-related charges add further pressure. How shore power cuts fuel use Shore power changes where a docked ship gets its electricity. Rather than keeping onboard generators running, vessels connect to the grid and switch those generators off. For Portsmouth, this provides a way to address air pollution from marine engines while supporting its broader environmental goals. The principle is straightforward: supplying electricity from the shore reduces the need to burn fuel onboard while a vessel remains docked. Portsmouth’s ambition sits alongside efforts at the ports of Long Beach and New York and New Jersey, as well as JFK’s Terminal One project, to make transport infrastructure cleaner. But the environmental and financial arguments depend on different factors. Switching off generators reduces onboard fuel consumption. Whether it also saves money depends on the price of the electricity purchased to replace that generation. Access to grid power therefore creates an alternative, rather than guaranteeing a cheaper option. A vessel operator still has to compare the cost of plugging in with the cost of keeping its generators running. At Portsmouth, expensive electricity makes that comparison challenging, even as the system offers a way to reduce pollution. Why electricity dominates the connection bill Electricity accounts for approximately 80–85% of the total cost paid by a vessel using shore power at Portsmouth. Port charges account for the remaining 15–20%. That breakdown explains why electricity prices matter so much. The larger share of the bill comes from purchasing power, rather than the port’s charges for using the system. Even though a connected ship avoids burning fuel in its generators, it must pay for the grid electricity taking its place. If that electricity costs more than onboard generation, reduced fuel spending does not translate into lower overall power costs. According to the House of Commons Library, UK electricity prices were 18% above the EU average in the second half of 2025. Separately, the International Energy Agency found that electricity prices for energy-intensive industries across the EU averaged more than twice those in the US. These comparisons illustrate the wider electricity pricing differences surrounding Portsmouth’s project. They help explain why the financial case for electrification can vary considerably between countries. For ships at Portsmouth, the immediate challenge is that cleaner power can cost more to operate. Rising grid charges complicate the economics Portsmouth faces an estimated 10% year-on-year increase in Transmission Network Use of System charges over the next five years. The increase concerns transmission charges, rather than the entire shore power bill. Nevertheless, it adds another cost pressure to a system already affected by high electricity prices. The source describes lower ownership costs for electric port equipment, including cranes, material handlers, terminal trucks and locomotives, compared with diesel equivalents. Hybrid-electric ships can also be cheaper in some uses. Those examples do not guarantee the same outcome for shore power in Portsmouth. Its system enables ships to reduce pollution while docked. Turning that environmental benefit into a financial saving depends on electricity prices and the grid-related costs accompanying them.

title: World’s highest bridge at 2,050 feet turns advanced steel truss into extreme tourism hub
content: The 9,482-foot-long Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in China has become a tourist attraction, with a glass observation hall, a narrow plank walk over the canyon, bungee jumping, and nighttime light shows. Originally designed to reduce a two-hour canyon crossing to just two minutes, it connects Guanling Bouyei-Miao Autonomous County with Zhenfeng County. In April 2026, c certified it as the world’s highest bridge , at 2,054 feet above the river below. Now, the bridge is a destination for sightseeing, adventure sports, and local tourism. During China’s recent week-long National Day Holiday, it drew thousands of visitors, highlighting the bridge as a tourist attraction that was always part of the plan. From engineering landmark to tourist attraction Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge opened to traffic on September 28, 2025, after three years of construction, according to Smithsonian Magazine , which reported on the opening on October 1, 2025. It surpassed the Beipanjiang Bridge , also known as the Duge Bridge which had held the world record since 2016 at about 1,854 feet above the river. The new bridge stood even taller at about 2,054 feet above the Beipan River. The entire Empire State Building could fit beneath it with about 600 feet to spare, as per the Smithsonian. The height was not really the point though. Chief engineer Yang Jian told Xinhua that they designed the bridge so high because if it were any shorter, they would have had to construct longer tunnels through the surrounding mountains, increasing costs and even contributing to driver fatigue. The design came from the need to balance the bridge length with the connecting tunnels, which is why it ended up so high. Tourism had long been integrated into the overall plan. Planners had assigned 50 square kilometers (19.31 square miles) around the bridge for that purpose. A maintenance passage was converted into a 2,611.55-foot sightseeing corridor. Engineers also incorporated a glass observation hall, an aerial sports platform, and a 1,411-meter (4,629 feet) elevated running track. Visitors can now take elevators into the bridge, walk along its sightseeing corridor and look out across the canyon above the river. Activities include bungee jumping, a suspended narrow plank walkway, and running along the elevated track. At night, water screen and light shows illuminate the bridge. For a special event such as the National Day Holiday, the bridge organized concerts, racing activities, and food events. Bungee jumping and glass observation decks The project has recorded about 3.3 million visits thus far, according to Xinhua . Some visitors have traveled considerable distances to experience the attractions. The bridge’s popularity has boosted tourism in the surrounding areas. Huajiang Township and nearby areas have received more than 1.48 million visits. Local businesses have benefited from improved transportation connections, and hotels are experiencing similar benefits. “Now that the bridge is open, rooms are often fully booked on weekends and public holidays. Visitors are coming, and they are willing to stay,” Wu Fuying, manager of Xiyuan Hotel in Huajiang Township told Xinhua. The bridge appears to be a win-win, facilitating transport and bringing tourists to the surrounding region in China, with visitors arriving to experience both the record-breaking structure and its range of attractions planned for the site.

title: Scientists stop a quantum particle using a magnetic field it never crossed
content: Quantum particles can move between two locations through a process called tunneling. However, what if a particle suddenly stopped moving because of a magnetic field it never directly interacted with? Physicists at the University of Oxford have recreated this counterintuitive behavior using a hybrid quantum computer, demonstrating the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a simulated quantum system. The Aharonov–Bohm effect occurs when a particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a change in its quantum phase, even though it never passes through the magnetic field itself. In the Oxford University experiment, this effect caused the particle’s possible paths to cancel each other out, completely suppressing its tunneling between two locations. These findings could help scientists simulate fundamental interactions that are increasingly difficult to model using conventional computers. Building a quantum loop from trapped ions In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, allows something more subtle. A particle can acquire a measurable phase change when it travels around a region containing magnetic flux, even if it never enters the region where the magnetic field exists. Physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted this effect in 1959, and experiments with real electrons later confirmed it. The Oxford researchers are now investigating how the same phenomenon behaves in lattice gauge theories, mathematical frameworks used to describe interactions between matter and fields in particle physics. In these theories, matter occupies points on a grid, while gauge fields connect those points. As these systems grow, calculating their behavior on conventional computers becomes increasingly difficult. Quantum simulation offers an alternative: researchers build a physical system that follows the same underlying rules as the model they want to study, then observe its behavior. Beginning in 2022, the study authors developed an experiment to simulate a lattice gauge theory, a framework for studying how matter interacts with gauge fields. Their hybrid system combined two components with different roles. Qubits, or quantum bits, encoded in the internal electronic states of trapped ions represented the gauge fields. Quantum oscillators, corresponding to the ions’ vibrations, represented matter. The researchers connected two oscillators, representing matter at two locations, using two qubits representing the fields between them. Together, these components formed a loop, an elementary building block of the theory. The team used digital operations to prepare and measure the system, while analog quantum evolution allowed it to simulate the interactions. The magnetic flux that canceled a particle’s movement The researchers prepared the two qubits in an entangled state , in which their quantum properties are linked in a way that has no classical equivalent. In the simulation, this state represented magnetic flux passing through the loop. Encoding the flux this way was initially a practical workaround. The hardware could not provide the interaction needed to introduce the flux as a fixed background. However, the approach also allowed the researchers to investigate something more interesting: a gauge field that could evolve alongside the matter it interacted with. “For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical. Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics,” Sebastian Saner, lead researcher and a postdoc researcher at Oxford University, said . The researchers then observed a matter particle tunneling between the two locations around the loop. Without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely. When the researchers introduced a flux, the two possible paths interfered destructively, canceling the tunneling process and leaving the system in its starting state. This is when “we observe Aharonov–Bohm interference with dynamical gauge fields encoding the magnetic flux, thereby demonstrating the interplay between charge and flux.” Extending quantum simulations to fundamental interactions The experiment offers a way to study how matter and magnetic fields interact in quantum systems. With further development, similar simulations could help researchers investigate more complex interactions that are difficult to model using conventional computers. In a related study, a team at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke, used a hybrid quantum system to simulate the Yukawa potential, an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics. Together, the studies show how hybrid quantum architectures could help scientists explore the fundamental forces and interactions that shape the physical world. The study is published in the journal Nature Physics .

title: 17-gigawatt Texas power project passes key hurdle for world’s largest private grid
content: A planned nuclear-powered supercomputing hub in the Texas Panhandle has cleared a major federal regulatory hurdle. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has published its draft environmental review for Project Matador, an energy and artificial intelligence campus run by developer Fermi America. Crucially, NRC staff issued a preliminary recommendation to approve combined licenses for four Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear reactors, provided the project passes an ongoing safety evaluation. The positive assessment arrived just 15 months after Fermi America filed its application. In the nuclear industry, federal environmental reviews typically take years to complete. Reaching this stage so quickly marks significant momentum for an initiative designed to power high-demand computing facilities. Proposing a new power outlook With Project Matador, the overall technology infrastructure could get a new outlook. It does not rely solely on the public grid. Instead, Fermi America is building a dedicated private system in Carson County, near Amarillo. The private network will combine commercial nuclear reactors with natural gas units, solar arrays, and utility-scale battery storage. Original plans for the site called for an 11-gigawatt (GW) campus, anchored by 4.4 GW of nuclear power. However, developers recently expanded their ambitions to nearly 17 GW. The upgrade aims to meet the relentless power appetite of next-generation artificial intelligence models and high-performance computing clusters, which require round-the-clock baseload electricity that intermittent renewables cannot supply alone. The site is being developed across 18 million square feet in partnership with Texas Tech University. Construction is scheduled to bring the facility online in stages, starting in the late 2020s and running into the mid-2030s. The federal recommendation builds directly on state-level regulatory wins from earlier this year. In February, Texas environmental authorities granted Project Matador a six-gigawatt Clean Air Permit . That decision stands as the second-largest air permit in US history, paving the way for the fossil fuel generation that will support the campus alongside its planned reactors. Clearing crucial regulatory hurdles Despite the recent progress, several crucial regulatory steps remain before safety-related construction on the nuclear reactors can begin. The NRC must complete and publish its final environmental impact statement. Simultaneously, regulators must complete a Safety Evaluation Report to verify that the standardized AP1000 design is compatible with the local geology, seismic conditions, and water resources. Only after both reviews conclude will the full Commission hold a vote on final license approval. Fermi America is advancing the complex design with several engineering and nuclear partners. The coalition includes reactor designer Westinghouse Electric Company, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, ENERCON, and Preferred Licensing Services. Largest private energy installations The project’s nuclear division is led by Mesut Uzman, alongside development leads Sezin Uzman, Andrew Bryant, and Dannie Weaver. If the remaining approvals follow smoothly, Project Matador will stand as one of the largest private energy installations in the world. It aims to bridge conventional nuclear engineering with the expanding power demands of the digital economy. “As Project Matador continues to advance, Fermi America remains focused on progressing through the remaining regulatory milestones and developing the energy infrastructure needed to power America’s AI future,” concluded the company.

title: Ultraviolet laser creates new defects in diamond without disturbing quantum centers
content: Deep inside a diamond, a misplaced atom or an empty spot in the crystal lattice could hold the key to better quantum technologies. However, changing one such defect without disturbing others while keeping the material useful has been a big challenge. Now, in a new study, researchers have used nanosecond ultraviolet laser pulses to modify diamond’s optical properties while leaving its existing nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers largely unchanged. This finding offers a potential way to engineer diamond’s defects more selectively. “Our study demonstrates that nanosecond laser pulses can achieve selective engineering of point defects in diamond and is promising for deterministic control of diamond color centers for quantum applications,” the researchers stated. Using ultraviolet light to manipulate diamond defects Diamonds consist of carbon atoms arranged in a crystal lattice. When atoms are displaced, missing or replaced by other elements, they create defects that can give the material new optical and electronic properties. One example is the nitrogen-vacancy center , which forms when a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom next to a vacant spot in the lattice. NV centers can function as quantum bits, or qubits, and serve as highly sensitive sensors of magnetic and electric fields. However, modifying one type of defect can also affect others nearby, making it difficult to tailor diamonds for specific applications. To investigate whether light could offer greater control, researchers irradiated a single-crystal diamond grown using chemical vapor deposition (CVD). They used 266-nanometer ultraviolet laser pulses, each lasting six nanoseconds, to expose localized regions of the crystal. The laser fluence—the energy delivered per unit area—ranged from 2.2 to 8.6 joules per square centimeter. Before irradiation, the team characterized the diamond using confocal photoluminescence spectroscopy, ultraviolet-visible absorption spectroscopy and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. These techniques helped establish the crystal’s initial optical defects, transparency and impurity content. The starting material contained very little substitutional nitrogen, in which nitrogen atoms replace carbon atoms in the lattice. Establishing this baseline was important: without it, researchers could not confidently distinguish defects associated with laser treatment from those already present in the diamond. New optical signals, but existing NV centers survive After irradiation, the researchers detected a previously absent photoluminescence signal near 563 nanometers in the exposed regions. A second emission appeared near 579 nanometers. Previous studies have associated these emissions with defects related to carbon self-interstitials, in which carbon atoms occupy positions outside their normal sites in the lattice. The more significant observation, however, was what did not change. The diamond already contained NV centers, and their optical signals remained largely unchanged after laser treatment compared with untreated regions. “We show that these nanosecond laser pulses can selectively engineer the 563-nm center, a self-interstitial-related defect, without affecting the background nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center,” the study authors said . This suggests that the laser can modify one part of the defect population without substantially disturbing another under the tested conditions. The distinction matters because the 563-nanometer and 579-nanometer centers have not been established as newly demonstrated qubits. Instead, the experiment points toward a possible way to engineer particular defects while preserving existing centers relevant to diamond quantum sensors . The researchers also found that the 563-nanometer emission did not increase indefinitely with continued exposure. Its signal could decline after reaching a maximum, suggesting that irradiation can both generate and transform defect configurations. The emission’s intensity showed a near-linear relationship with laser fluence, with a measured power-law exponent of 1.10 ± 0.16. This is consistent with a single-photon excitation process, rather than one requiring multiple photons to act together. What happens inside the diamond remains a mystery The precise atomic-scale mechanism is unresolved. The researchers propose that ultraviolet photons may excite electronic states associated with defects, with subsequent energy transfer potentially triggering rearrangements of nearby carbon atoms. Processes involving trapped charge carriers or excitons may also play a role, but the experiments did not establish the complete pathway or identify the exact atomic structures responsible for both emissions. The control over diamond’s optical properties as claimed in the study could eventually benefit quantum sensing and other devices that depend on carefully chosen defects. However, the study does not yet demonstrate a working quantum device or prove that a specific defect can be created on demand with complete reproducibility. The next step is to determine exactly how the defects transform and how consistently those changes can be controlled by adjusting laser conditions. If researchers can connect irradiation parameters to predictable atomic changes, they may eventually be able to design diamonds with tailored defect populations rather than treating their imperfections as an inseparable mixture. The study is published in the journal Diamond and Related Materials .

title: Troublemaker: US firm unveils 864-mile-range one-way attack drone
content: US defense contractor Ideal Aerosmith has unveiled Troublemaker, a Group 3 uncrewed aircraft designed to deliver long-range strike, surveillance and decoy capabilities without relying on runways or extensive support infrastructure. The company says the aircraft can fly for more than 10 hours, cover distances exceeding 750 nautical miles and carry payloads of up to 30 pounds, giving military operators a flexible platform for missions in contested environments.Troublemaker is designed to serve as either an expendable one-way attack drone or a recoverable aircraft that can be reused after a mission. Ideal Aerosmith adds that the aircraft can be launched from a catapult or truck and recovered using a skid landing system.Long-range drone built for flexible missionsAccording to specifications disclosed by company executive David Markert in an interview with Breaking Defense, Troublemaker has a wingspan of approximately 15 feet and a claimed range exceeding 750 nautical miles, or about 864 miles. Its payload capacity of up to 30 pounds gives operators room for different mission equipment, although Ideal Aerosmith has not publicly disclosed a unit price or detailed payload configurations.The aircraft is intended to support intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), long-range surveillance, decoy operations and one-way strikes. Its ability to be recovered after a mission that does not require its destruction could also help reduce operating costs, depending on the recovery process and the aircraft’s actual acquisition price.That flexibility is central to the concept of the drone. Instead of treating every aircraft as a single-use munition, operators could use the same platform for surveillance or deception missions and reserve expendable strike operations for situations where they offer a clear operational advantage. Furthermore, Ideal Aerosmith has also described Troublemaker as capable of operating in swarms. Coordinated groups of uncrewed aircraft could distribute surveillance, deception and strike functions across multiple platforms, potentially complicating an adversary’s ability to identify and prioritize threats. The extent of its demonstrated swarm capabilities still remains unclear, though, as company has not publicly detailed the system’s autonomy, communications architecture or performance in GPS-denied and electronically contested environments.Production capacity could determine its military valueIdeal Aerosmith says it has already built 26 Troublemaker aircraft and entered low-rate production at approximately two units per week. Markert told Breaking Defense that existing infrastructure could support production of as many as 20 aircraft per week if demand increases.That would represent a tenfold increase over the reported current production rate, although the higher figure describes potential capacity rather than funded orders or confirmed output. Ideal Aerosmith also looks to position Troublemaker within a broader US-based defense manufacturing effort, emphasizing supply chain security, modular design and scalable production. Markert added that Troublemaker has a Department of the Navy sponsor and that Ideal Aerosmith has responded to related government solicitations, although this does not confirm a formal procurement contract yet.With a claimed range of more than 864 miles and no need for a conventional runway, Troublemaker could give military units more options for launching surveillance and strike missions from remote or temporary sites. Its truck- and catapult-launch options may also suit maritime and expeditionary operations, while the ability to recover and reuse the aircraft could reduce the need to replace it after every mission.

title: US backs PowerLight’s ARC to wirelessly recharge drones mid-flight
content: US-based PowerLight Technologies has received an expanded investment from the Department of War to advance a field-deployable Aerial ReCharge (ARC) system.The follow-on award comes from the Department of War’s Operational Energy – Innovation (OE-I) Directorate. It builds on the ARC development under the PTROL-UAS program and the April 2026 demonstration at the Shaw Air Force Base.Drones are being increasingly used in modern warfare for short and long-range missions, including strikes, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions, and more. Their usage in other areas, such as monitoring oil pipelines and law and order, is also on the rise.One significant hurdle to drones being used more often is power. Battery-powered drones have to return to base after they run out of energy; this leads to a situation when there is either downtime for missions or multiple drones need to be utilized to fill the gaps.Increasing the mission time for military dronesThe battery life of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) is measured in hours. Every time a military drone returns to base, the recovery cycle includes an operator breaking cover, swapping its batteries, and then relaunching it in a risky environment.  The ARC system can therefore prove to be very useful in a contested environment for personnel on the ground. It uses laser power beaming to recharge the drones or their payloads in flight, which can drastically eliminate the problem.Whenever the drone’s battery needs a recharge, after reaching a set minimum point, the UAS can initiate a handshake with the ARC transmitter and recharge itself while still in flight. The drone can then return to carrying on its mission without having to make a landing.“Power beaming means more time on mission and less time on the ground,” OE-I Combat Power Portfolio Lead Chris DePuma said.He went on to add that by enabling autonomous, in-flight recharging, the Aerial ReCharge system reduces the need to land and swap batteries, extending mission endurance and reducing risk in contested environments.How does the ARC system work?The ARC system uses optical power beaming, which converts electricity into a precisely shaped beam of laser light that is transmitted through air, space, fiber, or water and converted back into electricity at the receiver.PowerLight says that the beam travels at the speed of light, carries no radio frequency signature, and can be sent over long distances.For demonstration, the ARC receiver was integrated into the Kraus Hamdani Aerospace K1000ULE, an ultra-long endurance drone. The U.S. Air Forces Central (AFCENT) had cleared the drone platform for use, and the ARC system is being matured on an aircraft the operators already fly.PowerLight’s engineering and test team is embedded at Shaw AFB, developing CONOPS and collecting data with AFCENT mission planners and operators during field testing to support transition to theater.“Power beaming applies well beyond a single domain, from ground-to-ground, ground-to-air, air-to-air, and space-to-space, and that is the opportunity ahead,” said Tim Jenks, CEO, PowerLight.

title: US Army upgrades LOADOUT logistics software after Iran war lessons
content: The US Army has upgraded its military transportation software based on lessons from Operation Epic Fury, aiming to give commanders a clearer picture of where cargo is, what transport capacity is available, and which movements need urgent attention.The updated system, called LOADOUT, manages requests to move military personnel, equipment, and supplies. The Army’s Combined Arms Support Command (CASCOM) developed the latest enhancements with theater sustainment commands and other operational partners after identifying a recurring problem. Soldiers were spending too much time chasing shipment updates instead of coordinating movements.A digital dashboard for military logisticsMoving military cargo involves more than assigning a truck or aircraft. Requests must be submitted, coordinated, matched with available transportation, executed, and eventually closed out. When information is scattered across different tools or requires repeated phone calls and emails, delays can add up.LOADOUT is designed to manage that process through a shared workflow for Transportation Movement Requests. Its latest version introduces customizable dashboards, line-by-line cargo-manifest exports, and improved tools for uploading and assigning organizational equipment lists and unit deployment lists.One important addition is an upgraded Movement Board that provides real-time visibility into available transportation capacity. A new Priority 1 banner also highlights mission-critical requests, helping users distinguish urgent movements from routine requirements.The goal is to give units and sustainment planners a common view of transportation demand and available capacity, rather than forcing each theater to rely on separate workarounds.Lessons from the war in IranThe changes follow Operation Epic Fury, which placed substantial demands on the US military’s global logistics network. Moving forces and supplies during a major campaign requires coordination across services, geographic commands, transportation hubs, and multiple supply routes.The Army says the LOADOUT updates were developed with the 1st Theater Sustainment Command, which supports operations in the Middle East, the 8th Theater Sustainment Command, US Army Forces, Japan, and other stakeholders.The wider campaign has also highlighted the value of faster, data-driven logistics planning. In April, reports surfaced that the US Transportation Command was expanding its use of real-time data and AI-enabled visualization to maintain visibility across the logistics network and evaluate alternative transportation options as conditions changed.Separately, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that Transportation Command used AI agents to assess alternative airfields after Spain restricted US military access to its bases and airspace in March. The tools helped planners compare factors such as aircraft parking capacity, ground operations, and access constraints.These are separate efforts from the Army’s LOADOUT upgrades, but they illustrate the broader push to make military logistics more responsive when routes, access, and transportation availability change unexpectedly.What comes next for LOADOUT?CASCOM held its first Functional Review Working Group for the software on September 24, bringing together leaders from the 1st and 8th Theater Sustainment Commands to review completed changes and establish future priorities.The Army plans to hold monthly reviews with theater partners. Potential additions include interim tracking for diplomatic and customs clearances, which can affect how quickly cargo crosses international borders.Over the longer term, the Army also plans to connect LOADOUT with its ARTEMIS capability suite so movement information can transfer automatically between systems.The current upgrades focus primarily on visibility, coordination, and workflow, not autonomous transportation or AI-driven cargo movement. Their value will depend on whether they reduce administrative friction and help logistics teams make better-informed decisions.For a military operating across vast distances, a clearer picture of transport requests and available capacity can be as important as the vehicles carrying the cargo. LOADOUT’s next test is whether those improvements translate into faster, more predictable movement of personnel and equipment when operational demands intensify.

title: US study finds first water cloud changes outside solar system
content: Water clouds are growing thicker and thinner on a frigid world just 7.5 light-years from Earth, giving astronomers a direct view of changing weather beyond the solar system.A team led by Brittany Miles at the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory used the James Webb Space Telescope to observe WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, for 11 hours. Collecting a spectrum every 15 minutes, the researchers distinguished shifting cloud cover from gases rising out of deeper atmospheric layers.Watching water clouds changeWISE 0855 sits near the boundary between brown dwarfs and giant planets. Brown dwarfs lack sufficient mass to ignite as stars and instead emit faint light from heat left over after their formation.At about twice Jupiter’s mass and nearly the same size, WISE 0855 resembles a free-floating giant planet. Its temperature is roughly 265 kelvins, or 17°F, placing it at the coldest end of the known brown dwarf population.“This is the first time we’ve been able to confirm that water clouds are becoming thinner and thicker on a nearby world,” University of Arizona researcher Brittany Miles said.“Before JWST, we only had photometry, which mixed up the effects of clouds, chemistry, and temperature all together. Now we can actually distinguish them,” she added. As the object rotates, regions with different cloud cover and temperatures come into view. Webb’s medium-resolution spectrograph tracked these variations across individual molecular features, allowing the team to separate atmospheric signals that earlier observations mixed together.Deep gases reveal atmospheric mixingThe observations revealed at least two processes operating simultaneously. Water clouds at high altitudes changed thickness, while convection carried chemical gases upward from deeper layers.Alongside temperature variations associated with rotation, the instrument detected a rhythmic, wavelike signal linked to carbon monoxide and phosphine. Heat inside the brown dwarf churns these gases upward, connecting its deeper atmosphere with the layers astronomers can observe.A similar process occurs on Jupiter, where convective mixing brings gases from hot, deep layers into the visible atmosphere. Known as disequilibrium chemistry, this behavior has previously been observed in brown dwarfs. Tracking its variations in real time across individual molecules adds another dimension.“We’re seeing water clouds getting thicker and thinner, and deep gases rising and falling, and we can actually watch them change in real time,” Miles said.A connection to giant planetsThe findings also offer a way to understand atmospheres beyond WISE 0855. Clouds, convection and chemistry link this cold object’s behavior to processes operating on Jupiter.“Even though brown dwarfs are not true planets, they exhibit planet-like behavior,” Miles said.Those similarities could help researchers interpret gas giant exoplanets observed with Webb, despite differences between individual worlds.Miles is looking toward additional baseline observations to clarify WISE 0855’s rotation and the three-dimensional movement of its atmosphere. Longer monitoring could sharpen the picture of how its clouds and gases change together.The research is available on the arXiv preprint server and has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal.

title: Amazon uses data from 1 million robots to power real-world machines
content: Amazon Web Services (AWS) has introduced an open-source development stack to help companies build and deploy robots that can perceive their surroundings, make decisions, and perform physical tasks by bringing together cloud computing, simulation, and artificial intelligence tools.Called the Physical AI Toolchain on AWS, the platform combines AWS infrastructure with NVIDIA’s physical AI software ecosystem to support the development of industrial robots, autonomous mobile machines, and humanoid systems. Amazon says the toolchain is intended to reduce the engineering effort required to move AI models from development into real-world machines.The launch reflects a broader shift in AI development: moving beyond systems that generate text and images toward machines that must interact with physical environments, where mistakes can damage equipment, disrupt production, or create safety risks.Teaching robots to operate beyond the screenTraditional industrial robots typically perform predefined movements in controlled environments. Physical AI aims to make machines more adaptable by enabling them to interpret sensory information, respond to changing conditions, and learn from experience.For example, a robot working on an assembly line might need to handle components presented at different angles, while an autonomous warehouse machine must navigate changing layouts and avoid obstacles. Humanoid robots face an even broader challenge: manipulating unfamiliar objects and performing tasks in environments designed for people.Training these systems requires more than a capable AI model. Developers need large quantities of training data, realistic simulations, computing resources, and methods to transfer trained models onto physical hardware.AWS says its new toolchain brings these elements together in a common development workflow, allowing companies to adopt the full stack or select individual components for existing projects.Five stages from simulation to deploymentThe toolchain is organized around five parts of the physical AI development process.Synthetic data generation: AI-generated environments create additional training scenarios without requiring every situation to be recorded in the real world.Model training: Systems learn from human demonstrations and simulated practice.Simulation and validation: Developers test robot behavior in virtual environments before running it on physical machines.Edge deployment: Optimized AI models run on deployed hardware, enabling real-time decisions without continuous cloud connectivity.Continuous improvement: Data gathered during operations can feed back into training, helping developers refine models for future deployments.The platform combines AWS services such as Amazon SageMaker for model training, Amazon EC2 GPU instances for simulation, AWS IoT Greengrass for edge deployment, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for orchestration.It also integrates NVIDIA tools, including Isaac Sim for robotics simulation, Isaac Lab for reinforcement learning, Isaac GR00T for humanoid robotics, and Cosmos for generating synthetic environments.The idea is to reduce the friction between these stages. Rather than assembling and maintaining every part of the development pipeline independently, engineering teams can use a shared architecture and adapt it to their hardware and applications.From warehouse robots to humanoid machinesAmazon says the toolchain draws on experience from its own robotics operations, which the company reports include more than one million robots across its network. That experience has exposed the practical challenges of operating autonomous machines at scale, from coordinating fleets to maintaining software across deployed hardware.The company highlighted several developers working on physical AI. NEURA Robotics is developing cognitive humanoid robots, RLWRLD is building foundation models for dexterous manipulation, and Config has built a pipeline for collect and expand robot-action training data.For manufacturers, the potential applications range from robotic arms that adapt to new assembly tasks to autonomous machines that move materials and monitor production. However, the toolchain is a development platform, not a ready-made robot, and its availability does not guarantee that a simulation-trained model will perform reliably in a factory or warehouse.Closing the gap between AI and physical machinesOne of the central challenges in robotics is the transition from simulation to real-world operation. A model that succeeds in a virtual environment may encounter unexpected friction, lighting changes, sensor noise, or variations in the objects it handles when deployed on physical hardware.By combining simulation, training, deployment, and feedback within one workflow, AWS and NVIDIA are aiming to make that transition easier to manage. The toolchain also includes fleet-management capabilities intended to help companies provision, secure, and update machines as deployments grow.For engineers, the significance is less about a single new AI model and more about the infrastructure needed to develop physical AI systems repeatedly and at scale. Whether the approach delivers on its promise will depend on how well it handles real-world variability, hardware differences, and the safety requirements of industrial deployment.

title: US' 100,000-ton aircraft carrier returns from Iran with new kill tally
content: After 321 days on deployment, the USS Abraham Lincoln has finally returned home. The ship departed San Diego on November 21, 2025, and returned to port on the 8th of this month, ending a long deployment just shy of the USS Gerald R. Ford’s 326-day record set in May 2026.Interesting in and of itself, but what has really caught attention is the very obvious kill tally daubed onto her superstructure. A common practice across many armed forces, the USS Abraham Lincoln appears to have been very busy during its six-month action with Iran.Images and videos released from US Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit show the ship (and her strike group) racking up an impressive roster of kills against various enemy assets. The most numerous appear to be one-way drone kills represented by Shahed-136 stencil markings.If the marks are to be taken literally, the carrier and her group are claiming they’ve neutralized 106 such drones during “Operation Epic Fury.” Other kills appear to include a claimed 34 surface vessels, 23 vertical missiles, and, interestingly, 10 submarines. Impressive tally for the USS Abraham LincolnThe kill tally also refers to around 1463 bombs/ordinance being deployed. All told, that would make a claimed kill record of about 173 individual targets. Kill tallies of this kind are a very common practice, especially for aircraft pilots who often paint small silhouettes on their aircraft’s fuselage after successful missions. But an important distinction is that the tally on the USS Abraham Lincoln is more likely a joint record for its strike group.This would include kills from various assets, including its aircraft complement and escort vessels. Importantly, these are also claims, not necessarily confirmed kills.For this reason, there appear to be some discrepancies in kill numbers from the claims made. The first is drones, where the strike group has only had an official citation for about 77, rather than the claimed 106. Surface vessels are also at odds with official records, seemingly underplaying its hand. According to official citations, the group sank around 64 surface vessels, not 34. As for submarines, there are no official citations. At the time of writing, it is unclear why this is the case. There are several plausible explanations, however. What’s in a number?For example, the stencils might include kills from different periods of the deployment, use different definitions of a kill, or only depict certain types of vessels. Alternatively, some may have been credited to specific aircraft or other units rather than to the strike group as a whole.As for the submarine kill claims, this is likely not referencing submarine-on-submarine engagements. It is known that prior to “Operation Epic Fury,” Iran’s navy operated a mix of Russian-made Kilo-class diesel-electric attack submarines and Ghadir-class midget submarines.Since it has previously been reported that Hellfire missiles and Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) ballistic missiles were used against such assets before, it is reasonable to conclude that this is what they refer to.In this case, the submarines were likely neutralized while surfaced or docked. Beyond the headlines, the strike group’s official citation from Hegseth shows an impressive record, including 3,693 combat flights and a total of 250 consecutive days at sea.

title: China’s BYD develops 18-foot luxury EV powered by solid-state batteries
content: For luxury electric cars, longer range often comes with a familiar compromise: a bigger battery adds weight. Solid-state technology could help ease that trade-off by storing more energy without requiring a heavier pack.BYD’s upcoming Yangwang executive sedan brings that possibility into the ultra-luxury conversation. Spotted testing in China, the roughly 5.5-meter (about 18 feet) vehicle combines coach doors and imposing proportions with reports that it could carry solid-state batteries.BYD has not confirmed that specification. While its appearance draws comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom, the battery question connects it to a broader development effort. BMW and Mercedes-Benz are already using electric sedans to investigate how advanced cells perform beyond the laboratory.What changes inside the battery?The difference begins with the electrolyte, which allows lithium ions to move between electrodes during charging and discharging. Conventional lithium-ion cells typically use a liquid electrolyte. All-solid-state designs replace that liquid with a solid material.This change can support electrode materials such as lithium metal, potentially increasing the energy stored for a given battery weight. For an electric car, that could mean longer range without simply adding more battery mass.Mercedes-Benz identifies higher energy density as a key benefit of its solid-state development work. Safety is another potential advantage. According to the US Department of Energy, solid electrolytes are less prone to leakage when damaged, although a complete battery’s performance still depends on its materials and construction. None of these possibilities establishes the Yangwang sedan’s range or charging speed. Those figures require confirmed specifications and testing.How Yangwang supports BYD’s luxury pushYangwang occupies the highest tier of BYD’s lineup, above Denza, and showcases technologies such as the company’s quad-motor e4 platform.The upcoming sedan extends that role into the executive segment. Its long wheelbase, boxy profile and coach doors introduce styling associated with established luxury flagships, giving BYD’s technological ambitions a more traditional exterior.Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing described it as “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.”The combination suggests a strategy built around luxury design and technological differentiation. A solid-state battery could strengthen that positioning, but its inclusion remains unconfirmed.What road tests actually demonstrateBMW announced in May 2025 that an i7 prototype near Munich was testing Solid Power’s all-solid-state cells. Engineers are examining cell expansion, pressure control and temperature management, with BMW acknowledging that further development is needed for a competitive complete battery system. Mercedes-Benz demonstrated another step in August 2025. An EQS prototype fitted with Factorial lithium-metal solid-state cells traveled 1,205 kilometers (748.8 miles) without recharging.Mercedes reported 25 percent more usable battery energy with comparable pack size and weight. These were development results, rather than specifications for a car available to buyers.Such tests show progress while revealing the engineering work still involved. For BYD, the next step is confirmation of what powers its flagship, followed by evidence that the battery can deliver alongside the luxury experience.

title: US Army replaces its aging rail fleet with specialized locomotives
content: The US Army is replacing aging locomotives and specialized rail equipment used to move military supplies with new deliveries designed around the unusual constraints of ammunition depots and military installations.The Army’s Tank-automotive and Armaments Command (TACOM) says more than one-third of its active locomotives have exceeded their expected useful life of 65 years. Its immediate goal is to reduce that proportion to below 20 percent, cutting maintenance costs and improving the movement of military equipment.The latest modernization effort has delivered two new locomotives and a specialized track-maintenance vehicle to three installations. The service says the locomotives are the first major additions to the Army’s rail fleet in more than a decade. Why military railways need specialized equipmentRailways remain an important part of military logistics, allowing the Army to move heavy equipment and supplies between installations, storage depots, and transportation hubs. The Army’s Transportation Corps notes that rail is routinely used to move much of the service’s equipment from home or mobilization stations to training areas and ports of embarkation.But military installations do not necessarily have the same track layouts and operating conditions as commercial rail networks. Older tracks, tight curves, restricted clearances, and limits on rail weight can make standard locomotives unsuitable for particular locations.That is why the Army’s latest purchases are not simply off-the-shelf replacements. The Army selected or configured each asset to meet the needs of the installation receiving it.Three deliveries address different problems120-ton locomotive: Crane Army Ammunition Activity, Indiana – $2.9 millionAccepted in February 2026, USAX 4673 was built by Knoxville Locomotive Works with special couplers and restricted exterior dimensions. These changes allow it to navigate tight track curves and limited clearances at the ammunition facility.80-ton switcher: Blue Grass Army Depot, Kentucky – $2.1 millionAccepted in October 2025, USAX 1699 was manufactured by SpecSys using the physical dimensions of a vintage General Electric 80-ton locomotive. The design allows it to operate on the depot’s older tracks, which have lower weight limits.Ballast regulator: Fort Drum, New York – $733,422Accepted in November 2025, this machine maintains the gravel bed supporting railway tracks and includes snow-removal attachments. It is intended to help crews maintain Fort Drum’s deployment railheads through harsh winter conditions.Equipment details and procurement costs are from the US Army’s recent October 2026 announcement.An effort to improve deployment readinessThe latest purchases follow years of reliance on older equipment. The previous major locomotive delivery identified by TACOM was USAX 6524, a 140-ton locomotive delivered to Fort Cavazos, Texas, in July 2015, for $1.84 million.TACOM is working with the US Department of Transportation’s Volpe National Transportation Systems Center, its primary procurement agency for the modernization effort. The partnership brings together Army logistics specialists, technical requirements, engineering reviews, and federal procurement processes.The effort also fits into a more expansive push to improve the readiness of the Army’s rail infrastructure. At an Army Rail Summit in 2026, service officials discussed the strain decades of operational demand have placed on locomotives, railcars, and installation track infrastructure, as well as the need for better visibility into equipment and track readiness.Replacing locomotives that have served for decades is only one part of that challenge. The Army also needs track-maintenance equipment and infrastructure capable of keeping railheads usable when deployment demands increase.The immediate target is to bring the share of over-age locomotives below 20 percent. Achieving it should reduce maintenance pressures and help installations move military equipment more reliably, whether for routine operations or a surge in deployment activity.

title: US firm’s new driverless military vehicle can outsmart drones
content: Moving military supplies through areas under fire puts drivers directly in danger. Forterra and Hypercraft are showcasing a driverless off-road vehicle designed for those missions at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington.The platform combines Hypercraft’s Razorback unmanned ground vehicle with Forterra’s AutoDrive self-driving system. It also carries a counter-drone turret from 9 Mothers, bringing autonomous resupply and drone defense onto the same vehicle.The companies describe contested logistics as a primary mission, although neither has announced a military customer, contract, or price for the combination.Forterra, previously known as Robotic Research, develops autonomy technology rather than manufacturing vehicles. AutoDrive combines software, sensors, and computers to enable existing vehicles to operate without a driver.A 4,000-pound payload without a driverRazorback is the first complete vehicle developed by Hypercraft, based in Provo, Utah. The company initially built electric powertrains for commercial vehicles before expanding into defense and unveiling Razorback earlier this year.Measuring more than 13 feet (4 meters) long, the vehicle can carry up to 4,000 pounds (1,814 kg), according to Hypercraft. The company reports a driving range of about 500 miles (800 km) and the ability to supply up to 38 kilowatts of electricity to external equipment.Its design accommodates third-party sensors, radios, weapons, and mission payloads. Hypercraft has already displayed Razorback with counter-drone radar from Fortem Technologies.“We’re going after contested logistics and other missions where a driver is the most exposed person on the battlefield,” Forterra Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders told Tectonic.“Razorback and AutoDrive combine to deliver a platform that can go further, over more complicated terrain, and power platforms in ways that traditional UGVs cannot,” he added. Autonomy built into the platformSanders said Razorback was designed for autonomy from the outset, making integration straightforward. He contrasted that approach with unmanned ground vehicles derived from crewed trucks fitted with self-driving equipment after production.According to Forterra, the system has been integrated into more than 50 vehicle types, used on over 1,100 missions, and placed under contract for more than 258 systems.Applications include Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicles used in Ukraine and Ford F-250 pickups for the U.S. Army. AutoDrive also equips Oshkosh Joint Light Tactical Vehicles used in the U.S. Marine Corps’ ROGUE-Fires anti-ship missile launcher.A shotgun turret for small dronesThe Razorback displayed at AUSA carries Edda, a roughly 50-pound (23 kg) counter-drone turret developed by Austin, Texas-based 9 Mothers.Edda detects the sound of small drone rotors, uses cameras to track targets and fires a shotgun. It is designed to engage drones approximately 7 inches (18 cm) across at distances between 33 and 328 feet (10–100 meters).In August, the U.S. Army tested the same turret on a self-driving Ford F-250 equipped with Forterra technology during a live-fire exercise at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.Forterra said its partnerships prioritize operational needs and production scalability, with autonomy requiring coordination across the vehicle, sensors, computers, communications, and operator. The Razorback pairing brings those elements together for contested resupply missions.

title: US plans ship-killing missiles for its strategic B-52 bomber jet
content: Plans are afoot to integrate the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile (LRASM) into the payload of the United States Navy’s fleet of B-52 “Stratofortresses.” According to reports, the Navy will contract Lockheed Martin to make this a reality.The plan, it seems, is to effectively turn B-52s into long-range, flying anti-ship missile silos. This would provide some interesting tactical options for the Navy, especially for conflicts with rivals, like China.It will also blend cutting-edge technology with one of its oldest, the now 70 year+ old B-52. First developed in the 1950s, this aircraft has an enormous weapon payload capacity and intercontinental range.The AGM-158C LRASM, in case you are unaware, is a stealthy, air-launched cruise missile. It is designed specifically to hunt and kill warships, including moving ships in contested environments.Old dog, new tricksCrucially, these missiles feature autonomous guidance, meaning they can independently hunt and destroy targets in a given “kill box.” This means they can be launched into a rough area to find potential targets without the need for specific coordinates. As it stands, the B-52 already carries the AGM-158 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile (JASSM), which is essentially the land-attack cousin of LRASM. In theory, this should make integration of the latter more straightforward than starting from scratch.That said, the targeting software and operational testing still require substantial work. Crucially, this is a planned integration contract, not an announcement that B-52s are already operationally equipped with LRASM.If successful, each B-52 should be capable of carrying similar payloads of LRASM as JASSM, which currently stands at around 20 per airframe. So, just a few LRASM-capable B-52s could provide a lot of potential firepower for the Navy to call upon if needed.“A handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy’s carrier-based aircraft per day,” retired Air Force Colonel Mark Gunzinger told Air & Space Forces Magazine.But why the need? Well, currently the Navy must rely on submarines, surface warships, and strike aircraft like its F/A-18 “Super Hornet” to deliver these missiles. Each has its advantages, but also its limitations.Carrier-based aircraft, for example, have relatively short unrefueled range, and ships have a finite missile capacity. Moving ships, like carriers, close enough to contested areas to fire such weapons is also inherently risky. Not without riskBut even integration into the B-52 won’t be foolproof. Each LRASM has a range of about 200 miles (320 km). That would mean that even if a B-52 took off from a base thousands of miles away, it still needs to get relatively close to launch its missiles.And the B-52 is not exactly the stealthiest of aircraft. For capable enemy forces like China, this would mean the B-52 would need supporting assets to either deflect attention away from them or directly protect them.“As a precise, stealthy and survivable cruise missile, LRASM provides multiservice, multiplatform, and multimission capabilities for offensive anti-surface warfare,” Lockheed Martin spokesperson Scott Swofford said. “By leveraging Lockheed Martin’s expertise in successful cruise missile productions, LRASM brings low-risk and long-term, flexible capabilities to the warfighters’ anti-surface warfare environment that no other inventory weapon provides,” he added.

title: US firm to commercialize autonomous freight rail $100 million funding
content: Parallel Systems has raised $100 million in a new funding round to scale production of its autonomous, battery-electric freight rail vehicles, betting that smaller, self-propelled railcars can make rail shipping more competitive with trucks on shorter routes.The Los Angeles-based company announced the close of its Series C round on October 7, saying the funding would support production of its third-generation Panther vehicle, commercial expansion, and entry into international markets. Founded in 2020 by former SpaceX engineer Matt Soule, Parallel Systems is developing a freight system that combines electric propulsion, autonomous control, and software-coordinated rail vehicles. Its aim is to make rail practical for shipments that are often moved by trucks because conventional freight trains are less flexible on shorter routes.Railcars that move without a locomotiveTraditional freight trains rely on locomotives to pull long strings of coupled railcars. That arrangement is efficient for moving large volumes over long distances, but assembling trains and coordinating terminal operations can make smaller, short-haul shipments less economical.Parallel’s approach is different. Its battery-electric vehicles propel themselves rather than relying on a conventional locomotive, and can operate individually or form coordinated groups, known as platoons. The vehicles can separate and regroup to route freight toward different destinations without requiring the same conventional coupling arrangements.The system is designed to carry standard shipping containers, allowing it to work with existing freight infrastructure and handling equipment. Onboard sensors and vehicle-control software track position and operating conditions, while the company’s software is designed to integrate with railroad control and logistics systems.The engineering challenge is not simply making a railcar electric or autonomous. It is coordinating multiple self-propelled vehicles while meeting railway operating rules and safety requirements, without sacrificing the energy efficiency that makes rail attractive in the first place.Testing moves beyond the laboratoryParallel is testing its technology in Georgia with short-line railroad operator Genesee & Wyoming under a Federal Railroad Administration-approved program.The pilot has progressed beyond an isolated test track. In September 2026, FreightWaves reported that the program had advanced to a phase involving a 30-mile stretch between Vidalia and an area east of Helena, Georgia. The broader testing program is intended to evaluate the vehicles and their operating approach under increasingly representative conditions.The company says several major railroads are now under contract to deploy its system for commercial freight transport. However, the Georgia program remains an important step in establishing how the technology will work within real railway operations.Making short-haul rail more competitiveParallel argues that its system could open routes that are currently difficult for conventional rail services to serve economically, particularly journeys under 500 miles. The company’s goal is to combine rail’s energy and cost advantages with more frequent departures and greater flexibility.Its website says the vehicles can travel up to 500 miles on a charge, although that is a company-stated capability rather than an independently established performance figure.The new funding will help Parallel scale Panther manufacturing and pursue international opportunities. The company has not disclosed a production timetable or the number of vehicles the Series C financing will fund.If the system can operate reliably at scale, it could give railroads another way to move containerized freight while reducing dependence on short-haul trucking. For now, the central test is whether autonomous electric railcars can move from supervised pilots to dependable commercial service across existing rail networks.

title: Autonomous combat drone capabilities to get expansion new funding boost
content: Ukrainian defense tech Buntar Aerospace has raised $16 million in a new financing round to expand production, develop its autonomous systems and enter new markets. The investment brings the company’s total capital raised to $30 million as it looks to build on its experience supplying reconnaissance technology to frontline units in Ukraine. The round was led by Freedom Fund and an international growth equity investor, with participation from Gardar, Iron Wolf and Autonomy Capital. Buntar plans to use the funding to increase manufacturing capacity, recruit engineering and operations talent, and expand beyond intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance into other defense and civilian applications.From reconnaissance drones to multi-domain autonomyBuntar’s existing business is built around two products: the Buntar-3 reconnaissance drone and Buntar Copilot, an AI-powered software system designed to support drone operations in combat. The company says the combination has established a growing customer base among Ukrainian frontline units.Its next step is to extend that experience into a broader range of autonomous defense systems. Co-founder Bohdan Sas said the company is focusing on missions that place heavy demands on skilled operators, including reconnaissance, counter-drone defense and precision-strike assistance.“We’re targeting the missions that depend most on highly trained operators: reconnaissance, counter-drone defence and precision strike assistance. That’s what Ukraine needs today, and what Europe must be ready for tomorrow,” Sas said in a statement.The main idea of the company is to automate parts of these missions so personnel can concentrate on operational decisions rather than manually managing every aspect of a drone’s flight or sensor operation. In turn, that could become vital as militaries deploy larger numbers of unmanned systems and face pressure to train operators faster.Buntar also plans to expand its dual-use product lines, applying technologies developed for defense to civilian markets. Autonomous systems have potential applications beyond the battlefield, although the company has not detailed specific new products or commercial markets it intends to enter.Ukraine’s defense industry faces a different R&D equationBuntar’s expansion comes as European defense technology attracts growing investor interest. According to figures cited in the company’s announcement from Dealroom, European defense-tech startups have raised $7.4 billion in venture capital this year, while drone startups have secured $4.7 billion across 40 funding rounds. US investors account for 47% of European defense-tech funding, highlighting the importance of international capital to the sector. For Ukrainian companies, however, building defense technology involves a different set of constraints from those faced by startups operating in more established procurement systems.Sas argues that Europe’s rising defense budgets should prioritize drones, software and trained operators rather than relying primarily on traditional military hardware. His argument reflects lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where unmanned systems have become central to reconnaissance, targeting and battlefield operations.Buntar says its new funding will help it expand manufacturing while continuing to invest in research and development, rather than treating product development and production as separate stages. The company’s longer-term ambition, however, is to evolve from a supplier of reconnaissance technology into a multi-domain defense autonomy business with international reach.
